title: React vs WordPress in 2026: Which Is Right for Your Business Website?
excerpt: WordPress still powers 43% of the web. React-based sites consistently outperform it. Here's an honest, jargon-free comparison to help you decide.

blocks.text: WordPress has been the default choice for business websites for 20 years. React — the JavaScript framework behind Facebook, Airbnb, and thousands of high-performance sites — has been reshaping what's possible for the last decade.

In 2026, the gap in performance, security, and long-term value between the two approaches is wider than ever. But that doesn't mean WordPress is wrong for every situation. This guide gives you an honest business-level view of the tradeoffs — without the developer evangelism.
What We're Actually Comparing

When people say 'React website', they usually mean a site built with Next.js — a framework that uses React to build fast, SEO-optimized websites. WordPress is a complete, self-contained CMS and website builder. They're solving the same problem from fundamentally different directions.

WordPress gives you a pre-built system you configure and extend. Next.js (React) gives you a blank canvas where every part is built intentionally. Both are used by millions of businesses. The right choice depends on your priorities.
Performance: Not Even Close
On raw performance, React-based sites win convincingly. Google's Core Web Vitals — the metrics that directly affect your search rankings — tell the story clearly:
These aren't edge cases. They're the reality of a WordPress site running 20–50 plugins, serving PHP-rendered pages from a single server, with images that haven't been properly optimized.

A Next.js site pre-renders pages at build time and serves them from a global CDN. There's no database query, no PHP execution, no plugin overhead when a visitor loads your page. The page is already built — it just gets delivered.

**Why this matters for your business:** Google uses Core Web Vitals as a ranking signal. A slow site ranks lower. And independently of rankings, 53% of mobile users abandon a site that takes more than 3 seconds to load. Every second costs you visitors — and conversions.
Security: Architecture Beats Configuration

WordPress is the most attacked CMS on the planet — not because it's badly built, but because it's everywhere. WordPress powers 43% of all websites, which makes it an irresistible target for automated attacks. In 2024, over 4 billion login attempts were made against WordPress sites monthly.

The attack surface is wide: the WordPress admin login is publicly accessible at a known URL, plugins frequently introduce vulnerabilities, and outdated PHP versions are common. Keeping a WordPress site secure requires ongoing vigilance: plugin updates, security plugins, two-factor authentication, regular backups.

A Next.js site has a fundamentally different security posture. There's no public-facing admin panel. No PHP execution. No plugin ecosystem to compromise. The site is static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript delivered from a CDN — there's nothing to attack in the traditional sense. Content management happens in a separate, purpose-built system (like Sanity or Contentful) that isn't connected to the public-facing site.
**The practical difference:** With WordPress, security is something you manage. With a modern static site, it's largely structural — built into the architecture.
Maintenance: Where Hidden Costs Live
This is where the total cost of ownership calculation often surprises business owners. WordPress looks cheaper upfront, but the ongoing costs add up.

The developer time spent keeping a WordPress site running smoothly — plugin conflicts, PHP version upgrades, security patches, performance firefighting — often amounts to 10–20 hours per year. At €100/hour, that's €1,000–€2,000 in maintenance costs before you've made a single improvement.
Content Editing: WordPress Has the Advantage Here

Let's be honest: WordPress wins on familiarity. Millions of people know how to use it. The block editor (Gutenberg) is genuinely capable. Plugins exist for almost everything. If your team is comfortable with WordPress and your site is simple, that counts for something.

Modern headless CMS platforms like Sanity are excellent — often better for structured content — but they require an adjustment period. Sanity's Studio is custom-built to your content model, which is powerful but means there's no out-of-the-box setup. Your development team configures it, then your editors use it.
For businesses with non-technical content teams making daily updates, the familiarity advantage of WordPress is real and shouldn't be dismissed. The transition to a new CMS has a learning curve.
SEO: Both Can Win, One Requires More Work

WordPress has excellent SEO tooling — Yoast and RankMath are genuinely good plugins. But WordPress's performance problems undermine the SEO gains from those tools. Google is penalizing slow sites. A WordPress site with 'good SEO settings' but a 40/100 PageSpeed score is fighting itself.

A Next.js site with proper metadata handling has excellent SEO capabilities built in. Server-side rendering ensures crawlers see fully rendered content. Performance scores in the 90s mean Google favors the site. The combination of technical SEO hygiene and raw speed gives a significant edge.

One nuance: WordPress sites with thousands of pages and long-established authority can still outrank newer Next.js sites on competitive terms. Domain authority built over years matters. But for new or relaunched sites, starting on a performant stack gives you a structural advantage.
Cost to Build: Honest Numbers

Next.js builds cost more upfront because they require more development skill and intentional architecture. But the total cost over 3 years often favors Next.js once you factor in reduced maintenance, better performance (fewer lost conversions), and no plugin licensing fees.
Which Is Right for Your Business?

**Choose WordPress if:** Your budget is tight (under €5,000), your site is simple, you or your team are already familiar with it, and you don't need high performance or heavy customization. A well-built WordPress site with a quality theme and minimal plugins is a reasonable solution for many small businesses.

**Choose Next.js (React) if:** You want a site that's fast by default, secure by architecture, easy to maintain long-term, and built to your exact requirements without compromise. You're investing in a business asset that should compound in value over 3–5 years. You're frustrated with WordPress performance, plugin conflicts, or constant maintenance overhead.

**The inflection point** is typically around €8,000–€12,000. Below that threshold, WordPress often makes sense. Above it, the case for a modern stack built on Next.js becomes compelling — because you're spending enough that you should expect the performance and longevity that comes with it.
One Test to Run Right Now

If you're on WordPress and wondering whether it's holding you back, you can find out in 60 seconds. Run your site through our free performance analyzer at [webvise.io/wp-health-report](/wp-health-report). You'll get your Core Web Vitals, PageSpeed score, and a plain-language breakdown of what's costing you rankings and conversions.
If your site scores above 85 on mobile, you're probably fine. If it's below 60 — and most WordPress sites are — you now have the data to make a decision.
